fig1_rdms_sidebar.png: Reproduced from Kriegeskorte et al. (2008), Figure 1. Two square dissimilarity matrices side by side, monkey IT on the left and human IT on the right, each with one row and one column per photograph, 92 in all. Thumbnails of the photographs run along the top and side, grouped and labelled: animate (human body, human face, non-human body, non-human face), then inanimate (natural, artificial). Colour gives dissimilarity as a percentile of one minus the correlation, from blue (0, similar) to red (100, dissimilar), on a colour bar at the right. In both matrices the animate images form a blue block at the upper left, with the deepest blue for faces, and pairs of one animate and one inanimate image are mostly red. Single neurons in a monkey and fMRI in people give matrices with the same block structure.
encoding_fit_heldout.svg: Computed: one monkey IT recording site (Bao et al., 2020) predicted from 512 units of an ImageNet-trained ResNet-18's late layer, with a random fifth of the images held out. Left panel: predicted response (vertical, about minus 5 to 45) against recorded response (horizontal, 0 to about 75), with a dashed diagonal where the two are equal. Training images are faint magenta dots, held-out images larger green dots; both spread along the diagonal, and the highest recorded responses are under-predicted. Labels: training R squared 0.71, held-out R squared 0.69. Right panel: R squared (0 to 1) against the penalty lambda on the squared length of the weight vector, on a log axis from 10 to the minus 2 to 10 to the 5. With almost no penalty, training R squared is 0.85 and held-out 0.28. As the penalty grows the training curve falls and the held-out curve rises; they meet near 0.69 at a dotted vertical line, the lambda chosen by cross-validation within the training images (about 562). Beyond it both fall. A readout is scored on held-out images, with its penalty chosen without them.
repetitions_majajhong.png: Computed from Majaj et al. (2015). Titled: The same image, 51 times (electrophysiology, monkey IT). Four stacked bar plots share a horizontal axis of recording site, 1 to 168, and a vertical axis of normalized response from minus 2.5 to 2.5. The top three rows, in blue, are single presentations 1, 2 and 3: each is a jagged pattern of bars reaching about plus or minus 2.5, and the three patterns differ site by site. The bottom row, in red, is the mean over all 51 presentations: its bars are much smaller, mostly within plus or minus 0.5, the largest about 1.3. One image never evokes the same response twice, so a model is fit to the mean, and the trial-to-trial variation is noise no model can predict.
splithalf_one_site.svg: Computed: a typical monkey IT site from Majaj et al. (2015), the one with median reliability. Scatter plot with one small red dot per image, 3,200 dots. Horizontal axis: the site's mean response over its odd-numbered presentations of the image, about minus 0.8 to 1.3; vertical axis: the mean over its even-numbered presentations, same range. A dashed diagonal marks equal values. The dots form a broad band along the diagonal with wide scatter around it. A label reads: one IT site, 3,200 images; r = 0.70; corrected 0.83. With no trial-to-trial noise every dot would lie on the diagonal. The correlation of the two halves, corrected to the full number of presentations, is the site's split-half reliability: the noise ceiling against which a model's score for this site is read.
tvsd_test_montage.png: Sixteen photographs from the THINGS database in two rows of eight, each with its concept name below: alligator, altar, ashtray, axe, bamboo, banana, beachball, bean; then beaver, bed, beer, bench, bike, blind, boa, boat. They are ordinary photographs of single objects or materials, some on plain backgrounds (an ashtray and a beach ball on grey) and some in natural settings (an alligator on rocks, a sailboat on a beach at low tide, pink and white feather boas). These are 16 of the 100 TVSD test photographs (Papale et al., 2025): the images each shown 30 times, on which the encoding models are scored.
tvsd_predictivity_by_block.svg: Computed: ImageNet-trained ResNet-50 on the TVSD test photographs (Papale et al., 2025). Line plot. Horizontal axis: the 16 blocks of ResNet-50 in order, grouped as layer1 (blocks 0 to 2), layer2 (0 to 3), layer3 (0 to 5) and layer4 (0 to 2). Vertical axis: median noise-corrected correlation over electrodes, 0 to 0.8. Colour gives the area, V1 blue, V4 green, IT magenta; line style gives the monkey, F solid, N dashed; shaded bands are 95% bootstrap intervals; a dot marks each curve's peak. V1 starts highest, near 0.64, and stays nearly flat until layer4. IT starts lowest, near 0.5, and rises through layer2 and layer3. V4 peaks at layer3 block 3 in both monkeys, about 0.68 in F and 0.71 in N. IT peaks later and higher: 0.76 at layer4 block 0 in F, 0.81 at layer3 block 4 in N. Every curve drops in the last blocks of layer4. Later areas are best predicted by deeper blocks, V4 before IT.
tvsd_rsa_vs_predictivity.svg: Computed: the same IT electrodes, test photographs and ResNet-50 blocks as the previous figure; monkey F solid, monkey N dashed, both magenta. Two panels share a horizontal axis of 16 blocks grouped into layer1 to layer4, and a vertical scale of 0 to 0.8. Left, titled Linear predictivity, IT: median noise-corrected correlation, rising from about 0.5 in layer1 to peaks of 0.76 at layer4 block 0 for F and 0.81 at layer3 block 4 for N, then falling slightly. Right, titled Representational similarity, IT: RSA, the Spearman correlation between the block's and IT's dissimilarity matrices over the 100 photographs. Both curves sit low, rising from about 0.13 (F) and 0.09 (N), with a dip at layer3 block 5, to peaks of 0.31 at layer4 block 0 for F and 0.16 at layer3 block 2 for N. A dotted horizontal line at 0.394, labelled Another brain (F to N), is the RSA between the two monkeys' IT. Both scores rise with depth, but on different scales, and they disagree on which monkey the network matches better.
pub_yamins2014_fig1a.png: Reproduced from Yamins et al. (2014), Figure 1A. Scatter plot with one dot per network, thousands in all. Horizontal axis: categorization performance (balanced accuracy), about 0.5 to 0.73, where 0.5 is chance. Vertical axis, labelled IT Explained Variance (%): the percentage of the IT sites' repeatable response variance that the network's top layer predicts, from below minus 15 to above 30. Colour marks how each network's settings were chosen: green, at random (r = 0.55); blue, by optimizing categorization (r = 0.78); orange, by fitting IT (r = 0.80). Green dots cluster at low accuracy, around 0 percent; orange dots reach the highest values, near 30 percent, at moderate accuracy; blue dots extend furthest right, rising to about 30 percent near accuracy 0.7. Two dashed grey lines at the right edge lead to the next panel of the paper. In every group, better recognition goes with better IT prediction.
pub_yamins2014_fig1b.png: Reproduced from Yamins et al. (2014), Figure 1B. Scatter plot. Horizontal axis: categorization performance (balanced accuracy), about 0.55 to 1.0; vertical axis: IT explained variance, 0 to 50 percent. Light blue open circles, many sampled networks, fill the lower left, up to accuracy 0.77 and about 34 percent. Black dots mark earlier models: Pixels near 5 percent, V1-like near 17, SIFT near 19, PLOS09 near 22, V2-like and HMAX near 26, all below accuracy 0.77. Red squares, the authors' HMO networks, climb toward the upper right; the best, labelled HMO, sits at about 0.98 accuracy and 50 percent. A purple square labelled Category Ideal Observer sits at accuracy 1.0 but only about 9 percent. A label gives r = 0.87 plus or minus 0.15. Dashed lines at the left edge link to the previous panel. The best recognizer predicts about half of IT's repeatable variance, while knowing the category alone predicts little.
pub_schrimpf2018_fig2_it.png: Reproduced from Schrimpf et al. (2018), Figure 2, IT panel. Scatter plot with one blue dot per network, each with a short vertical error bar. Horizontal axis: ImageNet performance, percent top-1, 40 to about 83. Vertical axis: IT neural predictivity, about 0.52 to 0.61, with gridlines at 0.55, 0.60 and 0.65. Predictivity rises from about 0.52 at 42 percent to about 0.60 near 70 percent, then stops rising. Labelled networks: alexnet at about 58 percent and 0.59; cornet_s, densenet-169 and densenet-201 near the top, at 75 to 77 percent and 0.60 to 0.61; resnet-152 and pnasnet_large, more accurate at 78 to 83 percent, lower at about 0.59; vgg-19 at about 71 percent and 0.57. A label gives r = 0.72. More accurate networks predict IT better overall, but the most accurate ones do not predict it best.
pub_conwell2024_fig5a_nolegend.png: Reproduced from Conwell et al. (2024), Figure 5A. Vertical axis: score, the Pearson correlation with human high-level visual cortex measured by fMRI, 0 to 0.8, with a thick grey line along the top at 0.8. Horizontal axis: more than 200 networks, sorted by score, best on the left. Filled dots are RSA after a linear fit to the voxels (veRSA); open dots are plain RSA (cRSA). The filled dark dots form a slowly sloping plateau from about 0.72 to about 0.6, annotated 126 Models within a Pearson r of 0.1; labels along it include ResNet50-CLIP, ResNet50-SimCLR, RegNet-64Gf-SEER, ResMLP-36, HardCoreNAS-F, ResNet50, ResNet50-RCNN-FPN, ConvNext-B, ViT-B-P16 and AlexNet. Their open dots scatter lower, between about 0.2 and 0.45. Then the scores fall steeply through pink and gold dots, annotated Drop in Score Largely Due to Input (Diet), to a tail of grey dots near 0.1, annotated Untrained Models. Very different architectures and objectives earn nearly the same score; the training images move it most.
pub_ahlert2024_fig1_rows.png: Reproduced from Ahlert et al. (2024), Figure 1, the four neural rows. A grid of numbers, each cell shaded red for a positive and blue for a negative correlation, deeper for larger values. Rows: V1, V2, V4 and IT predictivity. Columns, eleven measures: V1, V2, V4, IT, attention map similarity, i2n consistency, error consistency, odd-one-out similarity, shape bias, OOD (out-of-distribution) accuracy and ImageNet accuracy. Each cell is the Spearman correlation, across the networks tested, between the row's measure and the column's; the diagonal cells are 1.00. Between areas: V1 with V2 0.59, V1 with V4 0.34, V2 with IT 0.30, V4 with IT 0.35. The IT row against the seven behavioural measures, in order: 0.16, 0.09, 0.08, minus 0.26, 0.29, 0.21 and 0.09. The largest values off the diagonal are in the V4 row: 0.50 with error consistency, 0.52 with OOD accuracy, 0.56 with ImageNet accuracy. Measures of brain-likeness correlate only weakly across networks, some negatively.
pub_muzellec2026_fig3a.png: Reproduced from Muzellec and Kar (2026), Figure 3a. Scatter plot. Horizontal axis: forward predictivity, how well a network's units predict the IT sites, 0 to 70 percent explained variance. Vertical axis: reverse predictivity, how well the IT sites predict the network's units, 0 to 50 percent. A dashed diagonal marks equal values. Each network is a circle with error bars in both directions, coloured by family: CNNs, transformers, robust models, self-supervised (SSL) models and regularized models. Nearly all networks sit in one cluster far below the diagonal, from about 23 to 62 percent forward but only about 5 to 21 percent reverse. Two green circles, one monkey's IT predicting the other's and back, sit near the diagonal at about 37 and 42 percent. The comparison between two brains is symmetric, but networks carry many units that IT cannot predict.
pub_bashivan2019_fig2a.png: Reproduced from Bashivan, Kar and DiCarlo (2019), Figure 2A, one V4 site. Scatter plot of measured firing rate (vertical, minus 2 to 5, arbitrary units) against the model's predicted firing rate (horizontal, minus 2 to 8), with a dotted diagonal where prediction equals measurement. Blue dots, naturalistic images, and purple dots, complex curvature stimuli, lie along the diagonal between about minus 1.5 and 2.5. Five red dots, synthetic controller images, sit far to the right: predicted at about 6 to 7 but measured at about 3 to 4, higher than any natural image yet below the diagonal. Insets along the top show, in 8-degree circles, the best curvature stimulus (a white crescent), the best natural image and one synthetic image, each with an enlarged view of the small region inside the site's receptive field. Down the right side, five enlarged synthetic images, abstract grey patterns of rings, blobs and stripes, with a 1-degree scale bar. Images designed with the model drive the site past its natural range, though less than the model predicts.
pub_fel2022_clickme_4col.png: Reproduced from Fel et al. (2022). A grid of three rows, snake, bear and leopard, and five columns. Column 1: the photograph. Column 2, Human (ClickMe): the photograph darkened, with a yellow-green heat map of the regions people revealed most: a compact patch near one end of the snake's body, on the bear's muzzle and nose, and on the leopard's head. Columns 3 to 5: attribution maps for the same images from three networks, ViT, ResNet50 and Robust ResNet50. The ViT maps are scattered specks, many on the background; the ResNet50 maps are spread over the animal and the background; the Robust ResNet50 maps fall more on the animal, along the snake's body, on the bear's eyes and nose and on the leopard's head. The networks' maps are more diffuse than the human map and often highlight different regions.
pub_kamitani2005_fig2a.png: Reproduced from Kamitani and Tong (2005), Figure 2a. Eight polar plots in two rows of four, one per grating orientation shown: horizontal, then rotating in steps of 22.5 degrees through vertical to 157.5 degrees. A small black-and-white grating at each plot's top left shows the orientation. Dashed radial lines mark the eight possible orientations; a black line marks the orientation shown; a grey outline shows how often a readout of the fMRI responses chose each orientation, reaching farther along orientations chosen more often. In every plot the outline is elongated along the black line: the readout mostly chose the orientation shown. A label reads S2, V1/V2, 400 voxels. Orientation can be read out from the pattern across many voxels, although each voxel is only weakly tuned.
ringach_frame2_alexnet.svg: Computed from Ringach (2002) and AlexNet. Scatter plot comparing the shapes of receptive fields, each summarized by a Gabor fit. Horizontal axis: n_x, the fit's width in cycles of its grating, 0 to 1.4; vertical axis: n_y, its length in cycles, 0 to 1.4. Filled grey squares are 93 macaque V1 simple cells; open green circles are 32 of AlexNet's first-layer filters whose Gabor fit has R squared above 0.75. The cells spread along a rising band from the origin: many below 0.3 on both axes, others reaching about 0.8 wide and 1.4 long. The filters fall in two groups: a tight cluster near 0.2 wide and 0.1 long, and a broader group about 0.35 to 0.65 wide and 0.5 to 1.0 long that overlaps the cells, plus a few wider ones out to 1.3. The same two numbers place a cell and a network unit on one plot, where they partly overlap and partly differ.
hierarchy_meis_vs_physiology.png: Computed by the lab with MACO feature visualization (Fel et al., 2023), beside published physiology stimuli. Left, titled ResNet-50 units (feature visualizations): four rows of six square panels. Row conv1 shows six learned 7 by 7 first-layer filters as blocky colour images: colour-opponent blobs (orange against blue, green against magenta), a small checkerboard and vertical light and dark bars. Rows layer2, layer3 and layer4 show images optimized to drive one unit each: layer2, fine repeated textures such as scales, bubbles and weaves; layer3, larger repeated patterns and arches; layer4, crowded object-like parts that are harder to name. Right, titled what electrophysiologists show each area: for V1, three blurred oriented bars (horizontal, diagonal, vertical), credited to Hubel and Wiesel (1962); for V4, a grid of black curved silhouettes from Pasupathy and Connor (2001), one boxed in red; for IT, Tanaka's (1996) critical features, small black-and-white symbols grouped by cortical column. Nothing is shown beside layer2. The network's units go from edges to textures to parts, as the stimuli used for V1, V4 and IT do; the match is qualitative.
tics2026_neural_alignment.png: From Linsley, Feng and Serre (2026). Scatter plot of neural alignment, how well a network's features predict monkey IT responses (vertical, 0.2 to 1.0), against ImageNet multi-label accuracy (horizontal, about 0.45 to 1.0), several hundred networks drawn as coloured squares. Legend: CNNs trained on ImageNet-1K red, on internet-scale images pink, adversarially trained yellow; convolutional vision transformers (ConvViT) on ImageNet-1K dark green, internet-scale light green; vision transformers (ViT) on ImageNet-1K blue, internet-scale light blue, internet-scale vision and language grey. A grey vertical band labelled Human accuracy covers about 0.92 to 0.97. Two dashed lines meet near the band: one rising from about 0.5 at the left to about 0.7, one falling from there to about 0.6 at accuracy 1.0. Yellow adversarial CNNs sit at the left, accuracy 0.48 to 0.7; most red and blue networks cluster at 0.75 to 0.97 accuracy and 0.45 to 0.7 alignment. Purple stars mark recent models: SigLIP-2 and DINOv3 ViT-L near 0.65, DINOv3 ViT-H near 0.56, I-JEPA near 0.49, EVA-02 near 0.48 at the highest accuracy, and vJEPA2 lowest, near 0.29. Alignment rises with accuracy up to about human accuracy, then falls.
cnn_era_timeline.png: Line plot of ImageNet top-5 accuracy (vertical, 80 to 100 percent) against year (horizontal, 2012 to 2015) for five networks: AlexNet, 2012, 83.6 percent, 8 layers; ZFNet, 2013, 88.3 percent, 8 layers; GoogLeNet, 2014, 93.3 percent, 22 layers; VGG-16, 2014, 92.7 percent, 16 layers, a separate dot just below the line; ResNet-152, 2015, 96.4 percent, 152 layers, highlighted in yellow. A line joins AlexNet, ZFNet, GoogLeNet and ResNet-152. Top-5 accuracy counts an image as correct when the right label is among the network's five most probable. In three years accuracy rose by about 13 points while networks went from 8 to 152 layers.
pub_feather2023_fig1_metamers.png: Feather et al. (2023), Figure 2e. A grid of two rows and eight columns of small square images. The first column is a photograph of a dog. The next seven columns are model metamers for successive stages of a ResNet-50: conv1, layer1, layer2, layer3, layer4, average pooling, and the final output. Top row, the standard ImageNet-trained network; bottom row, a network trained semi-weakly on a billion extra images. For the early stages the metamer still looks like the dog; from layer3 on it becomes a texture of fur-like patches with no recognizable animal, and at the final stage it is close to noise, yet the matched stage responds to each metamer exactly as to the photograph.
pub_fel2022_alignment_vs_accuracy.png: Fel et al. (2022), Figure 3. A scatter plot with ImageNet top-1 accuracy in percent on the horizontal axis and human feature alignment in percent on the vertical axis, one marker per network: convolutional networks, transformers, self-supervised and robust networks, and networks trained with extra data, in different marker styles. A dashed curve traces the frontier of the ordinary networks: alignment falls as accuracy rises, from the oldest networks at the upper left to the most accurate at the lower right. Four harmonized networks (VGG, ResNet-50, EfficientNet and a vision transformer) sit well above the curve, each joined by an arrow to its unharmonized version: same accuracy, much higher alignment. A small dagger at the left edge marks the paper's control, the average ClickMe map used as every image's map.
pub_schrimpf2018_fig1_overall.png: Schrimpf et al. (2018), Figure 1. A scatter plot with ImageNet top-1 accuracy from 0 to 80 percent on the horizontal axis and the overall Brain-Score, from 0.35 to 0.55, on the vertical axis. Grey dots are hundreds of small networks built by architecture search; green dots are published deep networks, from AlexNet near 57 percent accuracy to networks near 80 percent. The cloud rises steadily: the correlation between accuracy and Brain-Score is 0.92.
featvis_hierarchy_4rows.png: A grid computed for the course with MACO (Fel et al. 2023). Four rows of networks: AlexNet, ResNet-50, ViT-B/16 and DINOv2 ViT-B/14. Three column groups of four units each: low layer, middle layer and high layer. The low column shows first-layer filters, not optimized images: oriented stripes and colour blobs for AlexNet and ResNet-50, noisy multicoloured patches for the two vision transformers. The middle and high columns show feature visualizations, images optimized to drive one unit, each a round patch fading at the edge. Middle layer: repeated textures and small curved motifs such as scales and dots. High layer: dense clusters of object-like parts, such as eyes and spiky shapes. The point: edges, then textures, then object parts, across the depth of every network.
topk_resnet50_layer4.png: Three ResNet-50 layer4 units, one per row. In each row, the unit's MACO feature visualization on the left, labelled with its number, then the six ImageNet validation images that drive it most strongly. Unit 43: a bronze helmet, a triceratops skull, a thatched roof, a burrito, a thatched cottage, and two axes on grass. Unit 179: a bell, small metal screws, a perforated bone, a bolt and a screw, a birdhouse, and a shark. Unit 309: piled sleeping bags, a volcano above a town, a volcano over a lake, a volcano in cloud, a tent below snowy peaks, and a yurt. The point: unit 309 responds to conical shapes, while unit 179 has no single label.
serre2026_annrev_fig4_ad.png: Four scatter plots from Serre 2026, Figure 4, of alignment score against ImageNet multilabel accuracy, 50 to 100 percent, for 363 image classifiers: CNNs as blue dots, transformers as orange dots, self-supervised and image-text models as open circles, adversarially trained models as triangles; a dashed line marks each dataset's ceiling. Panel a, Arcaro IT: rank correlation plus 0.37 over all models, minus 0.38 among the 84 above 92.7 percent. Panel b, Triple-N IT: minus 0.08 and plus 0.20. Panel c, TVSD IT: plus 0.73 and plus 0.65. Panel d, human feature use: minus 0.77 and minus 0.37; two harmonized models, VGG-16 and ViT-B/16, sit well above the cloud.
serre2026_annrev_fig4_e.png: Serre 2026, Figure 4e: five photographs, red fox, snake, hippopotamus, lizard, limousine, each with three heat maps: the human ClickMe map, a standard network's map, and a harmonized network's map. The harmonized maps coincide with the human ones on the animal's head or the car body; the standard maps are scattered or off the object.
